channel.title: Cairn
channel.description: Research into user interfaces where every action a person can take is a claim with a durable id and machine-checked evidence. Milestones and progress videos.

item.title: cairn-link links each dependency's libraries
item.description:
bin/cairn-link no longer links Cairn's library by name (#118). It reads lake-manifest.json, finds the cairn.toml beside each dependency, transitive ones included, and links the Lean libraries that package lists under libs. Cairn's own cairn.toml now lists Cairn, so an app gets the same archive as before, and a library like cairn_batteries can be linked the same way.

It refuses a Lean module that ends up in two archives, which would be a duplicate symbol, and a dependency that is an app. A dependency with no cairn.toml is linked not at all; if linked code imports it, cairn-link names the package and says to give it one.

Checked with a throwaway app that depends on Cairn and on a second library package with its own libs: it links, and a small C program draws a frame through both. Yap builds against it with its existing --lib Yap and passes its selftest.

As of commit 9ca784f, in the progress log of Third milestone: Pairs.

item.title: Third milestone: Pairs
item.description:
Can an app be built from packages alone, with images and requests it doesn't control? Pairs is a memory game: a grid of face-down cards, flip two, keep them if they match. Decks are theme packs, a JSON manifest and a set of images, from a folder or a URL. It is small enough to finish, and it needs what the Bluesky client after it will: images, JSON and many requests in flight at once.

  1. Images in Cairn: an image node whose size Lean knows before the pixels arrive, and an effect that loads one. The host decodes and paints; Lean never holds pixels.
  2. JSON as its own package, cairn_batteries, with a proof that decoding what was encoded gives it back.
  3. Requests in flight: at most 6 at once, and switching packs cancels the rest. A late reply for an old pack never changes the board.
  4. A grid that follows the window, proved for every width: no two cards overlap and every card is inside it.
  5. Proofs about the game: the deal has every face exactly twice, at most two unmatched cards are face up, and every game can be won.

Pairs lives in its own repository and is built only through the package path: cairn new pairs --bin, cairn add and cairn build.

Progress so far:

  • cairn-link links each dependency's libraries (2026-10-24)

item.title: Cairn 0.1.3, on the public registry
item.description:
Cairn 0.1.3 is out, and it is on the public registry at cairn.registry.nexthub.sh as iamnbutler/cairn, next to 0.1.2. Reading it needs no login: cairn add cairn finds the owner by name and writes the version range, and Lake fetches Cairn from the registry's git (#107, #109). /packages/ now reads the registry itself instead of sample data (#111).

The Cairn library is now only what an app links: 31 modules. Proofs, claims, fuzzing and tools are their own Lake libraries, so libcairn_Cairn.a went from 3.67 to 2.78 MB (#114). Three modules moved so the directories in lean/ have no cycles, and make lint now fails on one; the old names stay as shims until 0.2.0 (#110).

No claim changed, so it is a patch release. Yap moved to it with only its tag changed.

As of commit aea142c, in the progress log of Second milestone: Yap on Cairn.

item.title: Cairn 0.1.2: libraries and apps
item.description:
Cairn 0.1.2 is out. A package is now a library or an app, as in Cargo: cairn.toml has kind = "lib" or "bin", cairn new asks which, and /packages/ lists apps under their own tab (#103). Nothing can depend on an app.

cairn publish sends no docs. HTML from a publisher would run as the registry's site, so docs will be built from the source instead, as docs.rs does (#98).

The ledger now treats retiring a released claim as a breaking change: it needs a new major version, or a new minor one while at 0.x (#100). No claim changed in 0.1.2, so it is a patch release.

As of commit 597dea8, in the progress log of Second milestone: Yap on Cairn.

item.title: Cairn is a package, and Yap moved out
item.description:
Cairn is now a package. An app lives in its own repository and depends on a tagged release, and one tag pins both halves: the Lean package and the Swift libraries. v0.1.0 is the first release (#80). v0.1.1 fixes cairn doc, which failed in apps because it read its stylesheet from the app (#91).

Yap moved out first. It lives in its own repository, yap-cairn, and depends on Cairn v0.1.0 like any other app would. Its Lean, proofs, fuzzers, Swift host and benches left this repository with it.

Claim ids are now scoped by package. Cairn's are cairn^N and Yap's are yap^N, so “a shortcut never sends” is yap^311. Cairn's claims.lock still lists Yap's old ids, marked moved:yap, so they can never be issued here again.

As of commit ea72e75, in the progress log of Second milestone: Yap on Cairn.

item.title: The cairn command and packages
item.description:
There is now a cairn command (#79). cairn new starts a package in its own repository with its claim scope set, cairn add depends on another package, and cairn build runs Lake, links the Lean into one library and builds the Swift host. cairn doc writes the package's docs, and cairn publish and cairn login talk to a registry. It has unit tests, and it has been run against a stand-in registry but not a deployed one yet.

The registry is nextpm, a package registry, with a new cairn kind (nextpm #22). It has an index Lake reads natively, the source served over git, and a build cache, so that lake cache get downloads prebuilt Lean. Its claim ledger refuses a version that drops, renumbers or redefines an id. /packages/ shows a registry's packages, and until one is running it shows sample data (#78).

Publishers no longer upload docs. A registry now refuses HTML from a publisher (nextpm #23), and docs will be built from the source by a builder we run, the way docs.rs works (#94).

As of commit fb902c0, in the progress log of Second milestone: Yap on Cairn.

item.title: Developer docs and the API reference
item.description:
Developer docs are up at /docs, laid out like Rust's bookshelf: the Cairn Book, Cairn by Example, reference pages, and guides to working on Cairn itself (#76). Every code sample is included from a source file that make check compiles, so a sample can't drift from the code it shows. Moving an included region fails the build until the page is fixed.

The API reference at /docs/api/ is generated by cairn doc, Cairn's answer to rustdoc (#77). It reads the Lean environment directly instead of using doc-gen4. On TodoMVC, doc-gen4 took 185 s and wrote 227 MB, almost all of it Lean's own library. Each claim appears on its module's page with its statement, evidence and proofs. A Lean block in a doc comment is a doc test that make check runs.

Every heading on the site also has an id now, and a # that copies a link to it (#72).

As of commit d04416c, in the progress log of Second milestone: Yap on Cairn.

item.title: Yap against the original under Instruments
item.description:
Yap on Cairn was measured against the original Yap with Apple's Instruments rather than Cairn's own tools (#65). At 60 Hz the two overlays now pace the same, at 59.3 and 59.9 frames a second, with no hitches in either.

While recording, Cairn used 205 ms of CPU a second, against the original's 82. Most of that went to redrawing the menu bar's status item on every frame. Once its properties were written only when they change, an A/B run went from 197 to 98 ms/s.

The overlay now appears only once the microphone is running, as in the original, so a microphone that fails no longer flashes it (#68, yap^349). On a 120 Hz display, Cairn drew 118 frames a second where the original draws 60. It's now capped at 60, and it checks files every 2 s, as the original does (#69). The idle runs and a check on a 60 Hz display are still to do (#70).

As of commit 40b6863, in the progress log of Second milestone: Yap on Cairn.

item.title: Second milestone: Yap on Cairn
item.description:
Can claims hold up on real software someone uses every day? Yap is a small dictation app for the Mac: hold a key, talk, and the transcript is typed into the app in front. Almost all of it lives outside its window, so Cairn has to learn the outside world first.

  1. Effects: the clock and timers, requests the host performs and answers, and outside inputs like a global key and the microphone. Each one is a recorded assumption, fuzzed.
  2. New surfaces: a native menu bar menu built from Lean, and an overlay that never takes focus.
  3. Proofs about dictation: a shortcut never sends, a transcript is saved before it is typed, a late reply never types, every recording ends.
  4. Yap rebuilt on Cairn, signed and installed, and used for a real day of work.

Yap lives in its own repository now, yap-cairn, and depends on a tagged release of Cairn the way any app would. Getting it there made Cairn a package, with a cairn command and claim ids scoped by package: Yap's are yap^N.

item.title: First milestone: a proved TodoMVC
item.description:
1. The full TodoMVC app on the Mac, including real text fields and input methods.
  2. Every action is a claim with an id that the build refuses to let drift.
  3. Proofs: each action does what it says, the counts and filters stay right, and every control is present exactly when it should be and can actually be pressed.
  4. The real app is driven through a thousand generated sequences and must agree with the model.
  5. A map of the app, generated from the claims, showing the evidence behind each one.

Progress so far:

  • TodoMVC in Lean (2026-10-23)
  • Basics: the first Lean app (2026-10-23)
  • The host, with text (2026-10-23)
  • Boundary spike (2026-10-23)
